58.t: Trumpet styles: Buddy Petit, Rene, Ricard, Chris Kelly
58.s: Punch describes Petit's clean tone, Rene's high notes and Kelly's plunger work.
58.ch: Trumpet styles and early New Orleans scene
58.q: Well, I'm telling you, he had a wonderful style of playing at home. He wasn't a high note man, but he was, he had a wonderful tone and played everything clean. Real clean trumpet player. He was. Rene, he was a high note man. He went up in the air all the time. Ricard was turning out to be a nice…

58.t: Volume of Chris Kelly, Sam Morgan and Rena
58.s: Punch compares the volume of Kelly, Morgan and Rena, blaming Rena's small cup mouthpiece.
58.q: too well i'm gonna tell you sam morgan i don't think never had much volume chris did though chris test strong you know and uh renee was a good man for higher notes but he didn't have much of a volume neither he but he could you know make them higher notes uh i believe that was the cause of the…

175.t: Working with Kid Rena at the Gypsy Tea Room
175.s: He names early trumpeters and describes working with Kid Rena in 1932, his tone and easygoing life.
175.ch: Kid Rena, Kelly and the old trumpeters
175.q: But of course I would consider myself at that time not too much of a good judge of music or talent because I didn't know too much about it. But I could remember fellas like Buddy Petit and Sam Organ, old Sam Organ, and Chris Kelly, Kid Renee, and matter of fact I worked with Kid Renee for a while…

176.t: Kid Rene and Buddy Petit compared
176.s: De De says Kid Rene was his favorite, a fast-fingered high-range player of a better class of music, while Buddy Petit played ballhouse blues.
176.ch: De De's career and trumpet players
176.q: What would we call, what you say, well, what we call it here, Ballhouse. Buddy was more well, Ballhouse. In other words, he was rated higher class than the music line, you understand? Rene was. In other words, he played a better class of music.

999.t: Trumpeters who played at the fights: Thomas and Kyfer
999.s: He recalls David Thomas and Kid Kyfer, from Algiers, playing around the fights and Kyfer's small band.
999.q: Yeah Yeah I remember when David Thomas He was playing He was playing around the fights Yeah And always they say he would be a fine trumpet player He really turned out to be one too

178.t: Admired trumpeters: Cuckoo, Dumaine, Duran, Perez, Kid Rena
178.s: Ferbos recalls hearing Louis Dumaine, Maurice Durand, Manuel Perez and Kid Rena; Dejan tells of Rena's stamina at the Gypsy Tea Room.
178.q: Mm-hm. You know it might seem odd, but at that time, for like, what's his name? Cuckoo. Cuckoo. You know I used to like to hear Cuckoo play. And then now the Cuckoo is- Well Cuckoo was a pretty good trumpet. Yeah, he was a pretty good trumpet at that time. And what was his set up for there? Louis…

955.t: Buddy Petit, Kid Rene, Chris Kelly and Papa Celestin
955.s: He praises Petit's execution, Rene's round tone, Kelly's blues, and Celestin's sweet style, and says he joined Celestin's band shortly before his death.
955.q: Yeah, I played piano with Buddy. Buddy was one of the finest trumpet players. Now, he wasn't strong and powerful, but I mean, he had so much execution. I mean, to my, Buddy, Buddy had the time at the execution that they're using today. I think he's just that far ahead of time. I'd say, I'd put…

871.t: Kid Rene's trumpet and the Brown Derby; battle of the bands on trucks
871.s: Kid Rene played high above the staff and later worked with Bigard at the Brown Derby; bands used to buck against each other on the streets.
871.q: But not loud, they say. No, he wasn't quite loud, but he was pretty good. He was pretty good. Now what about other trumpet players there around the time you were playing with Buddy? Would they play a whole mamba or would they take it down? Oh yeah, you'd take like this little fella there, Kid René,…

183.t: Kid Rena's tone and why he never left New Orleans
183.s: Watts remembers second lining behind Kid Rena, praises his sweet tone and says he stayed in the corner bars rather than join Armstrong in Chicago.
183.q: Just so close, so walk with the, uh, Nero, My God, the D, and oh, they got some lovely numbers. Just barely walking. And each man playing his part, like the first trumpet, the second trumpet, like that. You know, getting all the harmony out of it, you know. Oh, that's the most beautiful thing.…

1000.t: Punch Miller, Kid Rena's tone, and working with Rena
1000.s: Punch and Rena were popular and good; Rena had a sweet tone, and Gallaud turned down a late job with him at the Cadillac when Rena was ill.
1000.q: He was pretty good at that time. He was pretty good. Punch and, what you call him? Oh man, oh man, that was goody good at that time.

625.t: Trumpeters on the trucks: Rena, Alcorn, Clifford Brown and Armstrong imitators
625.s: Trotter recalls bands on the trucks with Kid Rena, Alvin Alcorn and Clifford Brown, and Allen and Trotter discuss trumpeters copying Armstrong.
625.q: Alvin Alcorn, cause he was playing with Tyrone. Alvin used to play a lot on the short bands, cause he always was using Alvin. He was a good man, you know. Always used to use Alvin. Would Hange use a trumpet on the trucks? Oh yes. Who'd he get on the trumpet? Well, sometime he'd have Alvin with him,…

251.t: Buddy Petit, Kid Rena and Chris Kelly; their influence
251.s: Albert recalls visiting Buddy Petit in a one-room shack and praises him, Kid Rena and Chris Kelly, whose plunger work Cootie Williams took. He compares Punch Miller, Billy Douglas and Louis.
251.q: I can remember the trees and the green shrubbery. A few homes. Beautiful homes sitting in these, under these great big trees. Of course, you had the slum area over there. Well, now I wouldn't say slum. I hate to use it. Yeah. But, for instance, Buddy B.T. lived in the great trumpet players about…

264.t: Buddy Petit compared with Kid Rene, Evan Thomas and Louis Armstrong
264.s: Petit contrasted with high-note player Rene, Evan Thomas and Louis Armstrong; Zardis recalls Bunk and Baker duets and says all respected Petit.
264.ch: Opening and the Buddy Petit band
264.q: And you take Bunk, I mean that Bunk, this boy Yvonne, and we used to have a tenor player called Baker. You know? You ever met Baker? No, never met Baker. That's two men. Well I mean we used to work together. I mean duets, you know what I mean? Both of them up there high, trumpet high and that…

875.t: Kid Rena and comparing favourite trumpeters
875.s: Howard praises Rena's big, clean tone and again names Chris Kelly and Armstrong as favourites.
875.q: Yeah. But he was wonderful. He was really good. Yeah, really good. I was Paul Barrett for a year when he died.

475.t: Kid Rena's style and Shulky following him
475.s: Discussion of Kid Rena's high-note style and how Shulky, who followed the band around, played just like him.
475.q: Shulky. Well a couple of other people mentioned it. I was going to ask if it was Shulky. If you listen to Shulky. If you listen to Shulky you hear Renee. People tell me he used to follow the band around.

634.t: The Rene kids' brass band repertoire and Rene's playing
634.s: The Tulane played patriotic marches by hand; Rene's kids played juke music; Rene was a sweet cornet player but afraid to travel.
634.q: Well they played a few numbers. Like, you know, like the band playing now. They played a few numbers by hand. But those days, they mostly, mostly played patriotic band. Six eights and all that. That's what the brass band played.

1006.t: Comparing Buddy Petit and Rene, trumpet rivals at the Eli and Lauderdale
1006.s: Alexis compares Petit with Rene, names trumpet players around Iberville, and recalls playing for Beans with Black Benny and Willie Humphrey.
1006.q: Better than Rene for ragtime? Oh no, no. He wasn't. They were... I mean they both had top notch bands. Uh huh. Rene was a high note man, just like I was. High note. They talk that every day right now in the city. They talk that by Mueller's ball, I'll bum every day right now. Uh huh. That's Rene…

881.t: 1921 visit to New Orleans, Rene's C-sharp blues and Armstrong's Chloe
881.s: On his first return home he heard Rene, then talks about keys, Armstrong's Chloe solo and Mud Carrier.
881.ch: Becoming a player; Rene, Bunk and Armstrong
881.q: Well then, I'll tell you what happened. I've forgotten about this. I returned in the Orleans in 1921. That's when I met Chester's artists. They were advertising. And I rode on the truck. While I'm still in the preliminary stages. So. You hadn't played any jobs yet. Well I played some with a little…

84.t: Lyric Theater, drummers and New Orleans trumpet and trombone players
84.s: He recalls the Lyric Theater crowd, drummer Black Benny, and assesses trumpeters like Buddy Petit and Dude Foster and trombonist Yank.
84.ch: Armstrong, the Elite and New Orleans scene
84.q: Well, he was a summons on him, Red Happy. He used to, he was with John Robichaud. Oh man. He was a fine drummer, this guy, Black Benny, was a fine drummer. He got killed, a poison or something. I think he got killed. He had some nice trumpet players around here like Buddy Petit, Ricka, Rene, Chris…

197.t: Kid Rena and bands on the Pelican stage
197.s: Never worked with Chris Kelly or Kid Rena but heard Rena; his sidemen, the Hot Six records and praise for his trumpet.
197.q: well no I never did work with Kid Renee but I used to be around where he played that because he played on that story and we were playing across the street from that story during that time I was with the Handys band

801.t: Playing before his father's death; Kid Rena
801.s: Eddie says he began before his father died in 1919 without playing in bands. After the death Simon took over, and Eddie praises Kid Rena as a cornetist.
801.q: Yeah. When I stopped, it was, Kate Renee, that after my daddy died in nineteen nineteen, my brother Simon took six.

825.t: Kid Rena's style and the Gypsy Tea Room band
825.s: Kid Rena was more modern than Petit, powerful, strong in the high register and in all keys. He never let a band member down, and Dejan recalls the Gypsy Tea Room band.
825.ch: Early freelance work and New Orleans trumpeters
825.q: oh yeah yeah of course he came a little bit after him not much but he was more modernistic than what they were see and he had plenty of power oh he was powerful this is like kid renee you speak yeah kid right here they say he was very good in the high register he was he could start off on high and…

307.t: Chris Kelly, Punch and Buddy Petit's playing; learning from records
307.s: He praises Chris Kelly's blues and plunger mute, Punch's trumpet variations and Buddy Petit and Kid Rene, and says he learned clarinet parts from Armstrong and Fazola records.
307.q: Yeah, he was fast, yes. Punch could variate that trumpet. I never saw a man variate the trumpet that much like Punch used to do it. And I mean some wonderful notes he'd come out that horn, you know, and he'd go. He'd do some wonderful variation. He'd behead me skint on the clarinet at the time. I…

997.t: Buddy Petit, Kid Rena and Sharkey Bonano
997.s: He names Buddy Petit and Kid Rena as favourite high trumpeters and says Sharkey Bonano used to listen to Rena and plays close to him.
997.q: No. Just ordinary loud trumpet players. You all have to get anything on the old man Petit? Not much. Not much. Not much. I don't see how you all did. I don't know anything much about him, playing around here, but that's before my time. But when I was playing, he was still living though.
